issues.legal_issue: Acquisition of property for a genuine public purpose is not legally malicious merely because it is initiated after the acquiring authority has lost eviction proceedings and been directed to vacate the property.
material_facts: The State had occupied the school building as a tenant for many years and had operated a school there to serve children in the surrounding area.
The owner obtained eviction orders and a direction requiring the State to vacate, and the State had undertaken to deliver possession.
The State initiated acquisition proceedings shortly before the extended period for vacating expired.
The acquisition was for continuing the school’s service to the educational needs of children in the area.
issues.conclusion: The timing of the acquisition, following the eviction orders and direction to vacate, did not establish legal malice because the acquisition served a genuine public purpose; the proceedings were not a colourable or mala fide exercise of power.
issues.legal_principle: Legal malice by the State means action taken without lawful excuse, for an oblique or indirect object, or for a purpose not authorised by the governing law; it does not require personal ill-will. The State’s tenant rights are distinct from its sovereign power of eminent domain. Under Sections 4(1) and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, acquisition for a genuine public purpose may be pursued even after the State has lost its position as tenant. State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh recognised the State’s power of eminent domain; State of U.P. v. Keshav Prasad Singh and First Land Acquisition Collector v. Nirodhi Prakash Gangoli support the conclusion that acquisition is not mala fide merely because it follows adverse court orders where the public purpose is real and not a camouflage. State of U.P. v. Hindustan Aluminium Corporation did not assist the owner on these facts.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and existing_public_service and eviction_orders_against_acquiring_authority and acquisition_for_continuing_public_service and not foreign_or_camouflaged_purpose

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The case challenges the acquiring authority’s use of compulsory acquisition to obtain property.
predicates.existing_public_service: The property was already being used to provide a public service to people in the surrounding area.
predicates.eviction_orders_against_acquiring_author: A court ordered the acquiring authority to vacate property that it occupied as a tenant.
predicates.acquisition_for_continuing_public_servic: The acquiring authority pursued acquisition so the public service being provided from the property could continue.
predicates.foreign_or_camouflaged_purpose: The acquisition was pursued for a purpose unrelated to the asserted public service, or the asserted purpose was a camouflage.

issues.definition: When a compulsory-acquisition challenge concerns property already used for a public service, acquisition for continuing that service is not legally malicious merely because eviction orders preceded it, provided the asserted purpose is not foreign or a camouflage.

issues.legal_issue: A public purpose for acquiring an existing school property is not defeated solely because the property does not conform to standards applicable to proposed new school buildings.
material_facts: The school had operated at the location for many years and served the educational needs of children in the area.
The State relied on the continued educational use of the property as the purpose for acquisition.
The owner argued that the school premises did not meet standards fixed for setting up a school.
The standards relied on were made applicable after the acquisition proceedings and were not necessarily applicable to existing school buildings.
issues.conclusion: The asserted nonconformity with standards for setting up a school did not invalidate the acquisition or negate the public purpose served by the existing school at that location.
issues.legal_principle: The existence of a public purpose is assessed in light of the actual public service being provided; standards for proposed new school buildings need not necessarily apply to existing buildings. The Court applied the principles of eminent domain recognised in State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh and relied on State of U.P. v. Keshav Prasad Singh and First Land Acquisition Collector v. Nirodhi Prakash Gangoli concerning acquisition for a real public purpose. Sections 4(1) and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act were the provisions under which the acquisition was initiated.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and existing_school_serves_local_educational_needs and standards_apply_to_new_buildings and not evidence_public_service_is_unreal

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The case challenges the acquiring authority’s use of compulsory acquisition to obtain property.
predicates.existing_school_serves_local_educational: An existing school on the property provides education to children in the surrounding area.
predicates.standards_apply_to_new_buildings: The standards relied on concern proposed new school buildings and are not shown to govern the existing building.
predicates.evidence_public_service_is_unreal: The evidence shows that the claimed educational service is not genuinely being provided or that the stated public purpose is a camouflage.

issues.definition: When an existing school serves local educational needs, nonconformity with standards applicable to new buildings does not negate the public purpose unless the service is shown to be unreal.

issues.legal_issue: Temporary relocation of a school from a dangerous building does not by itself extinguish the public purpose for acquiring the building and its premises.
material_facts: The school building was old, dilapidated, and found to be dangerous.
The school had been shifted to an alternative site to avoid the risk of the building collapsing.
The acquisition had been pursued to enable the State to continue serving the educational needs of children in the area from the existing location, including through repairs or reconstruction.
issues.conclusion: The school’s temporary relocation for safety reasons did not establish that the public purpose had ceased to exist, and the acquisition could not be set aside on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: A temporary change in the location of a public service to address an immediate safety risk does not, without more, show that the public purpose underlying an acquisition has ceased. The Court applied the genuine-public-purpose and eminent-domain principles recognised in State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh and relied on State of U.P. v. Keshav Prasad Singh and First Land Acquisition Collector v. Nirodhi Prakash Gangoli. Sections 4(1) and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act governed the acquisition; the Court also declined the requested intervention under Article 136 of the Constitution.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The case challenges the acquiring authority’s use of compulsory acquisition to obtain property.
predicates.public_service_relocated_temporarily_for: A public service operating from the property was moved temporarily to avoid a safety risk at the property.
predicates.property_can_support_continuation_of_pub: The property can be repaired, altered, or rebuilt to support continuation of the public service.
predicates.public_purpose_remains_genuine: The public service underlying the acquisition remains a genuine purpose rather than a camouflage.

issues.definition: When a public service is moved temporarily for safety and the property can support its continuation, the move does not extinguish a still-genuine public purpose.
